drapeaux.note: Langue du texte fourni : français ; auteur d'origine : Giorgio Vasari (Vite, texte original italien de 1550). Retraduite depuis le français ; « Jean de Bruges » rendu par « John of Bruges » (Vasari : Giovanni da Bruggia).

titre: Van Eyck Did Not Invent Oil Painting
accroche: In 1550, Vasari writes that Van Eyck invented oil painting. Monks were already practicing it three centuries earlier.
contenu_vulgarise:
## A Painting That Cracks in the Sun

According to Vasari, Van Eyck once left a painted panel to dry in the sun. The wood supposedly split at the joints. Furious, the painter then supposedly looked for a medium that no longer feared heat: oil. The anecdote is precise, dated (around 1410), and false on the point that matters. Van Eyck invented nothing.

## A Legend Written 160 Years Later

Giorgio Vasari publishes his *Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects* in 1550, about 160 years after Van Eyck's death. He never saw him paint. He records an oral tradition and names “John of Bruges” the first inventor of oil painting. No author before him, not even the most attentive Flemish chroniclers, had made this claim.

A first rebuttal comes as early as 1774. The German writer Gotthold Ephraim Lessing comes across an unpublished manuscript by a 12th-century monk, Theophilus, and publishes an essay that dismantles the legend from the text itself. Theophilus's treatise, *De Diversis Artibus*, composed around 1100-1120, gives precise recipes: grind pigments in linseed or walnut oil in order to paint. Three centuries before Van Eyck was born.

Science pushes the date back much further still. In 2008, a team including the Japanese researcher Yoko Taniguchi, commissioned by UNESCO to study these paintings, and the French chemist Marine Cotte, analyzes with synchrotron radiation the paint layers of the Buddhist caves of Bamiyan, in Afghanistan. Twelve caves yield drying oils, walnut and poppy, used as a binder on wall paintings from the mid-7th century. A thousand years before Van Eyck, oil is already serving as a binder for painting.

## What Remains True, Once the Myth Is Set Aside

One question remains: why does his name stick so well to the process, if the process already existed? Because what he masters is not oil itself, but a way of using it that no one before him had pushed so far. He layers several coats of almost transparent glazes, each laid over a dry underlayer, mixing drying oils and resins with a goldsmith's precision. The result: a depth of light and a rendering of materials, fur against stone, velvet against metal, that no other European workshop was producing at the time.

Van Eyck therefore did not open up a technique. He showed what it could render. The question “who invented oil?” has no good answer, so old and diffuse is the practice. The one that matters is different: who was the first to draw from it a light that no one had yet seen painted.

carte.punch: He is credited with inventing oil. Afghan wall paintings were using it in the 7th century.
carte.idee: In 1550, Vasari makes Van Eyck the inventor of oil painting. A 12th-century monk already described the recipe, and Afghan Buddhist caves bear traces of it from the mid-7th century. Van Eyck perfected glazing; he did not invent the binder.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: ESRF — Synchrotron light reveals oil in the Buddhist paintings of Bamiyan
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The report, by the European synchrotron (ESRF), on the analysis that identified the drying oils in the Bamiyan caves.
A sourced overview of the history of the process, from Theophilus to Van Eyck and beyond.

quiz.question: Why does Van Eyck's name remain attached to oil painting, when monks were already using it three centuries before him?
choix: Because he is, historically, the first painter to have mixed a pigment with a drying oil
Because Vasari names him “first inventor” in his Lives of 1550, and his glazing in layered coats remains without equivalent in Europe
Because Theophilus's treatise on oil as a binder was found and published only in the 20th century
Because the 2008 dating of the Bamiyan caves has since been invalidated by new analyses
quiz.explication: The attribution comes from Vasari (1550), not from any real priority: Theophilus describes oil as a binder as early as the 12th century, and the Bamiyan caves yield oil paintings from the 7th century. What remains unprecedented in Van Eyck is his mastery of glazing in layered coats.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Vasari publish the claim that Van Eyck invented oil painting?
choix: In 1550, in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters
In 1410, during Van Eyck's own lifetime
In 1774, in an essay refuting the legend
In 1100, in a treatise by a Benedictine monk
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text dates the publication of Vasari's Lives to 1550, about 160 years after Van Eyck's death, so he could never have watched him paint.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is the first to refute Vasari's legend, and on what basis?
choix: Marine Cotte, in 2008, thanks to synchrotron imaging
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, in 1774, thanks to Theophilus's manuscript
Yoko Taniguchi, in 2008, on behalf of UNESCO
A Flemish chronicler contemporary with Van Eyck
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text credits Lessing, in 1774, with discovering the treatise of Theophilus, a 12th-century monk who already described oil as a binder for pigments.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the synchrotron radiation analysis of the Bamiyan caves reveal in 2008?
choix: That Van Eyck had traveled to Afghanistan before painting
That the Buddhist monks used the same recipe as Theophilus word for word
That oil painting was born in China before reaching Europe
That drying oils served as a painting binder as early as the mid-7th century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the team of Taniguchi and Cotte identifies drying oils, walnut and poppy, as a binder on Bamiyan wall paintings dated to the mid-7th century.
